grammar.title: Countable and uncountable nouns with quantifiers
grammar.summary: Countable nouns (an egg, two eggs) have a plural form. Uncountable nouns (rice, water, advice) have no plural and don't take a/an. The noun type decides the quantifier: many and a few go with countable nouns, much and a little with uncountable nouns, and a lot of, some and any go with both.
grammar.summaryMn: Тоологдох нэр үг (an egg, two eggs) олон тоотой. Тоологдохгүй нэр үг (rice, water, advice) олон тоо болон a/an авдаггүй. Хэмжээ заах үгийг нэр үгийн төрлөөр сонгоно: many, a few — тоологдох нэртэй; much, a little — тоологдохгүй нэртэй; a lot of, some, any — хоёуланд нь.
structure: Countable: an egg · two eggs · How many eggs? · many / a few / not many eggs
Uncountable: rice · some rice · How much rice? · much / a little / not much rice
Both: a lot of / lots of / some / any / no + plural countable or uncountable noun
some → positive sentences, offers and requests · any → negatives and most questions
Counting uncountable nouns: a glass of water · a slice of bread · a piece of advice

usage.use: many and much mostly in questions and negative sentences
usage.example: How much coffee do you drink? — Not much. How many eggs are there? — Not many.
usage.useMn: many, much-ийг ихэвчлэн асуух болон үгүйсгэх өгүүлбэрт хэрэглэнэ

usage.use: a lot of / lots of in positive sentences, with both types of noun
usage.example: I eat a lot of fruit and lots of vegetables.
usage.useMn: Эерэг өгүүлбэрт a lot of / lots of хэрэглэнэ — тоологдох, тоологдохгүй аль алинд нь

usage.use: a few (countable) and a little (uncountable) = a small amount, but enough
usage.example: Add a few tomatoes and a little oil.
usage.useMn: a few (тоологдох), a little (тоологдохгүй) — бага зэрэг, гэхдээ хангалттай

usage.use: some in positive sentences, offers and requests; any in negatives and questions
usage.example: Would you like some tea? Sorry, there isn't any sugar.
usage.useMn: some — эерэг өгүүлбэр, санал болгох, гуйхад; any — үгүйсгэл, асуултад

usage.use: Containers and units make uncountable nouns countable
usage.example: Can I have two glasses of water and a slice of bread?
usage.useMn: Сав, хэмжээ заасан үгээр тоологдохгүй нэрийг тоолно

examples.note: Milk is uncountable (much); eggs are countable (a few).

examples.en: We've got a lot of vegetables, so we don't need to buy any.
examples.note: 'A lot of' in a positive sentence; 'any' in a negative one.

examples.en: How many cups of coffee do you drink a day?

contrast.with: much vs many, a little vs a few, a few vs few

pairs.a: How much water do you drink a day?
pairs.b: How many glasses of water do you drink a day?
pairs.why: Water is uncountable, so 'much'. Glasses are countable, so 'many'.
pairs.whyMn: Water тоологдохгүй тул much, glasses тоологдох тул many.

pairs.why: 'Time' is uncountable; 'minutes' is a plural countable noun.

pairs.a: I have a few friends here, so I'm happy.
pairs.b: I have few friends here, so I feel lonely.
pairs.why: 'A few' = some, enough (positive). 'Few' without 'a' = not many, not enough (negative).
pairs.whyMn: 'A few' — цөөн хэдэн, хангалттай (эерэг утга). 'a'-гүй 'few' — бараг байхгүй, хангалтгүй (сөрөг утга).

mistakes.wrong: Can you give me an advice?
mistakes.right: Can you give me some advice?
mistakes.why: 'Advice' is uncountable: no 'an' and no plural. Say 'some advice' or 'a piece of advice'.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Advice' тоологдохгүй тул 'an' болон олон тооны -s авахгүй. 'some advice' эсвэл 'a piece of advice' гэнэ.

mistakes.wrong: How many money do you spend on food?

I eat a lot of vegetables.
mistakes.why: 'Vegetables' is countable, and in positive sentences 'a lot of' is the natural choice.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Vegetables' тоологдох нэр; эерэг өгүүлбэрт 'a lot of' хамгийн байгалийн сонголт.

mistakes.right: I bought two loaves of bread.
mistakes.why: 'Bread' is uncountable in English. Count it with 'a loaf of' or 'a slice of'.
mistakes.whyMn: Англи хэлэнд 'bread' тоологдохгүй. 'a loaf of' (бүтэн талх), 'a slice of' (зүсэм)-ээр тоолно.

grammar.title: should, shouldn't and ought to for advice
grammar.summary: Use should + base verb to give advice or say what is the right thing to do. Shouldn't means 'it's a bad idea'. Ought to means the same as should; it is less common and is used mostly in positive sentences.
grammar.summaryMn: should + үйл үгийн үндсэн хэлбэрээр зөвлөгөө өгч, юу зөв болохыг хэлнэ. Shouldn't — 'хийхгүй байсан нь дээр, муу санаа'. Ought to нь should-тэй ижил утгатай, арай бага хэрэглэгддэг бөгөөд ихэвчлэн эерэг өгүүлбэрт орно.
structure: should / shouldn't + base verb: You should rest. You shouldn't skip meals.
ought to + base verb: You ought to see a doctor. (For the negative, use shouldn't.)
Questions: Should I take a painkiller? What should I do? — Yes, you should. / No, you shouldn't.
Softer advice: I think you should… · I don't think you should… · Maybe you should…

usage.use: Saying that something is a bad idea
usage.example: You shouldn't eat so late at night.
usage.useMn: Ямар нэг зүйл муу санаа гэдгийг хэлэх

usage.example: What should I eat before a run?

usage.use: Saying what is right or expected
usage.example: Children should eat plenty of vegetables.
usage.useMn: Юу зөв, зүй ёсны болохыг хэлэх

usage.use: Making advice softer and more polite
usage.example: I think you ought to rest. / I don't think you should go to work.

examples.en: You should drink a lot of water when you have a temperature.
examples.note: Friendly advice, e.g. from a pharmacist.

examples.en: You shouldn't take more than eight tablets a day.
examples.note: Shouldn't = it's a bad or dangerous idea.

examples.en: We ought to eat more fish — it's really good for us.
examples.note: Ought to = should. It's less common in questions and negatives.

examples.en: Should I go to work tomorrow? — No, I don't think you should.
examples.note: 'I don't think you should' sounds more natural than 'I think you shouldn't'.

pairs.b: You must take this medicine twice a day.
pairs.why: 'Should' is advice — it's your choice. 'Must' is a strong rule or something really necessary, e.g. from a doctor.
pairs.whyMn: 'Should' — зөвлөгөө, сонголт таных. 'Must' — заавал биелүүлэх хатуу шаардлага (жишээ нь эмчийн заавар).

pairs.a: You shouldn't eat so much salt.
pairs.b: You mustn't drive after taking this medicine.
pairs.why: 'Shouldn't' = it's not a good idea. 'Mustn't' = it's not allowed or it's dangerous.
pairs.whyMn: 'Shouldn't' — тийм ч сайн санаа биш. 'Mustn't' — хориотой эсвэл аюултай.

mistakes.why: After 'should', use the base verb without 'to'.

mistakes.wrong: You don't should eat so late.
mistakes.why: Don't use do/don't with should. Add 'not': should not / shouldn't.
mistakes.whyMn: Should-тэй do/don't хэрэглэхгүй. Үгүйсгэлд shouldn't гэнэ.

mistakes.wrong: Do I should call a doctor?
mistakes.why: In questions, put 'should' before the subject. No 'do'.

pronunciation.title: Linking: a lot of, a bit of, a glass of
pronunciation.explanation: In natural speech, when a word ends in a consonant sound and the next word starts with a vowel sound, we join them together. 'A lot of' sounds like 'a lo-tof', and 'a cup of tea' sounds like 'a cu-pof tea'. The word 'of' is usually weak: /əv/. Linking makes your English sound smoother and easier to follow.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Үг гийгүүлэгч авиагаар төгсөж, дараагийн үг эгшиг авиагаар эхэлбэл бид хоёр үгийг холбож, нэг үг мэт дуудна: 'a lot of' → 'a lo-tof', 'a cup of tea' → 'a cu-pof tea'. 'of' ихэвчлэн сул /əv/ гэж дуудагдана. Ингэж холбож хэлбэл яриа тань илүү жигд, ойлгомжтой сонсогдоно.

items.tip: The t joins the next vowel: /əˈlɒtəv/.

items.display: a glass of water → a glas‿sof water
a piece of cake → a pie‿sof cake

items.tip: The d moves to the start of 'eat'.
Three links in a row — say it like one long word.

shadowing.text: I drink a lot of water and eat a bit of fruit every day.

shadowing.tip: Link 'lot of' and 'bit of': a lo-tof, a bi-tof.

shadowing.text: Would you like a piece of cake and a cup of tea?
shadowing.stress: Would you LIKE a PIECE of CAKE and a CUP of TEA?

shadowing.text: I've got a bit of a cough, but I'll get over it.
shadowing.stress: I've got a BIT of a COUGH, but I'll get Over it.
shadowing.tip: 'bit of a' → bi-to-va; 'get over it' → ge-to-ve-rit.

shadowing.stress: You should EAT a little LESS and WALK a lot MORE.

spokenForms.note: Very informal speech only. Never write 'lotta' in an email or essay.

lessons.title: Thirty days without sugar
objectives: Use 12 words and collocations for diet and healthy eating

warmup.intro: Think about what you ate yesterday. Was it healthy?

questions.prompt: Which of these is usually the healthiest snack?
The blog in this lesson is called 'Thirty Days Without Sugar'. What do you think the writer did?
options: She stopped eating food with added sugar for a month.
She ate only sweets for thirty days.
She went on a thirty-day holiday.

vocabulary.definition: the food that you usually eat
examples: My diet is much healthier than it was five years ago.
A diet with a lot of vegetables is good for your heart.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'be on a diet' or 'go on a diet' (to lose weight) — not 'do a diet' or 'make a diet'.
vocabulary.note: 'Diet' means all the food you eat, not only a plan to lose weight.

vocabulary.definition: containing the right amounts of different things
examples: A balanced diet includes fruit, vegetables, protein and a little fat.
It's hard to eat a balanced meal when you're always in a hurry.

vocabulary.definition: full of the things your body needs to be healthy and strong
examples: Soup is cheap, quick and very nutritious.
Growing children need nutritious food.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't confuse 'nutritious' (good for your body) with 'delicious' (tasty). A cake can be delicious but not very nutritious.

vocabulary.definition: (of food) changed in a factory, often with added salt, sugar or chemicals
examples: Sausages, crisps and instant noodles are all processed foods.
I try to eat less processed food and cook more at home.

vocabulary.definition: containing a lot of sugar
examples: Sugary drinks are bad for your teeth.
The kids ate too many sugary snacks at the party.
vocabulary.note: Similar words: salty (a lot of salt), fatty (a lot of fat), spicy (hot, with chilli or spices).

vocabulary.definition: a small amount of food that you eat between meals; to eat between meals
vocabulary.mn: хөнгөн зууш, хоол хооронд идэх юм
examples: I usually have a small snack, like an apple, at about four o'clock.
Try not to snack in front of the TV.
vocabulary.mistake: As a verb, use 'snack on': 'I snack on fruit', not 'I snack fruit'.

vocabulary.definition: a very strong wish to eat or have something
vocabulary.mn: ямар нэг юм тэсэхгүй идмээр санагдах хүсэл
examples: I get a craving for chocolate every afternoon.
The cravings stopped after about two weeks.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'a craving for chocolate' — not 'a craving of' or 'a craving to chocolate'.

vocabulary.definition: to stop doing, eating or drinking something that you did regularly
examples: I gave up sugar for a whole month.
My dad gave up smoking ten years ago.
vocabulary.mistake: After 'give up' use a noun or -ing: 'give up smoking', not 'give up to smoke'.

vocabulary.definition: to eat, drink or use less of something
examples: I'm trying to cut down on coffee.
The doctor told him to cut down on salt.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't forget 'on': 'I'm cutting down on sugar', not 'I'm cutting down sugar'.
vocabulary.note: 'Cut down on' = less, not zero. If you stop completely, you 'give up' something.

vocabulary.definition: to not eat a meal, or not do something that you usually do
examples: I often skip breakfast because I'm in a hurry.
Skipping meals can make you very hungry later.
vocabulary.note: Also used for classes and activities: 'skip a lesson', 'skip the gym'.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of food that one person eats at one time
examples: Restaurant portions are often too big.
I've started eating smaller portions at dinner.

vocabulary.definition: a piece of paper on a product that gives information about it
examples: Always read the label before you buy a new food.
The label says there are 30 grams of sugar in this bottle.
vocabulary.note: A nutrition label shows the calories, sugar, fat and salt in a product.

reading.title: Thirty Days Without Sugar
text: Last January I made a decision that surprised my friends: I gave up added sugar for a whole month. I wasn't overweight, but I often felt tired after lunch, and every afternoon at about four o'clock I had a terrible craving for something sweet. I usually had a chocolate bar or a few biscuits with my coffee, and I drank a lot of fizzy drinks.

The first week was the hardest. I started reading the label on everything I bought, and I was shocked. There was sugar in bread, in pasta sauce, in yoghurt and even in some sausages! Most of the processed food in my kitchen contained sugar, so I started cooking more at home.

My diet changed a lot. Instead of sugary snacks, I ate an apple or a handful of nuts. I stopped skipping breakfast, because on the days when I skipped it, I always ate too much at lunch. I tried to make every meal balanced and nutritious, with plenty of vegetables and some protein, and I made my portions a little smaller.

By the third week, the cravings were almost gone. I had more energy in the afternoon, and I was sleeping better. Did I lose weight? Yes, about two kilos, but that wasn't the most important thing for me.

Now the month is over, and I'm not so strict. I still have a piece of cake at a birthday party. But I've cut down on sweets a lot, and I don't drink fizzy drinks any more. My advice? Don't try to change everything in one day. Start with one small thing, like the sugar in your tea.

speaking.prompt: Mini cooking video: present a simple dish from your country. Say what ingredients you need and how much, then explain the main steps.
speaking.promptMn: Богино хоол хийх видео: өөрийн орны энгийн нэг хоолыг танилцуул. Ямар орц хэр хэмжээгээр хэрэгтэйг хэлээд, хийх үндсэн алхмуудыг тайлбарла.
points: Name the dish and say when people eat it
List the ingredients with quantities (a few, a little, some, a lot of)
Explain three or four steps (chop, fry, boil, stir)
phrases: Today I'm going to show you how to make…
speaking.sample: Hi everyone! Today I'm going to show you how to make tsuivan, a very popular Mongolian dish of noodles with meat and vegetables. For four people you need about half a kilo of flour, a little water and a pinch of salt for the noodles. You also need some beef or mutton, one or two onions, a few carrots and a little cabbage. You don't need much oil — about two spoons. First, make the dough, roll it very thin and cut it into long noodles. Next, chop the meat and vegetables and fry them for a few minutes. Then add a cup of water, put the noodles on top and cook everything with the lid on for about fifteen minutes. Finally, stir it well and serve it hot. It's simple, but it's full of flavour — and the leftovers are great the next day!

examples: A high temperature is a common symptom of flu.
If the symptoms don't go away, see a doctor.

vocabulary.definition: a pain in your throat, often when you have a cold
examples: I've got a sore throat, so I can't sing today.
Hot tea with honey is good for a sore throat.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't forget 'a': 'I've got a sore throat', not 'I've got sore throat'.

vocabulary.definition: to push air out of your throat suddenly with a loud noise; this illness or sound
examples: I couldn't sleep because I was coughing all night.
That's a bad cough — you should see a doctor.
vocabulary.mistake: Pronounced /kɒf/: the 'gh' sounds like 'f', as in 'enough'.

vocabulary.definition: if you have a temperature, your body is hotter than normal because you are ill
examples: She stayed at home because she had a temperature.
The nurse took my temperature.
vocabulary.mistake: To say you are ill, use 'a': 'I have a temperature', not 'I have temperature'.
vocabulary.note: British 'have a temperature' = American 'have a fever'.

vocabulary.definition: having a bad reaction to something, like a food, an animal or a plant
examples: I'm allergic to nuts, so I always check the ingredients.
Some people are allergic to cats.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'allergic to', not 'allergic for' or 'allergic on'.
vocabulary.note: The noun is 'allergy': 'I have an allergy to nuts.'

vocabulary.definition: a medicine that reduces pain
examples: Take a painkiller if your headache gets worse.
I don't like taking painkillers unless I really need them.
vocabulary.mistake: In English we 'take' medicine and painkillers — not 'drink' or 'eat' them (Mongolian 'эм уух').

vocabulary.definition: a piece of paper from a doctor that says which medicine you need
examples: You can't buy this medicine without a prescription.
The doctor gave me a prescription for antibiotics.
vocabulary.mistake: Mongolian uses 'жор' for both, but in English a 'recipe' is for cooking and a 'prescription' is for medicine.

vocabulary.definition: feeling that everything is turning round and you might fall
examples: I felt dizzy when I stood up too quickly.
The heat made her feel dizzy.

vocabulary.definition: to start to have an illness, usually not a serious one
examples: I think I'm coming down with a cold.
Half the class came down with flu last week.
vocabulary.note: Informal and very common in speech. 'I'm coming down with something' = I'm starting to feel ill.

vocabulary.definition: to become healthy again after an illness
examples: It took me two weeks to get over the flu.
Are you getting over your cold?
vocabulary.mistake: No 'from' after 'get over': 'get over a cold', not 'get over from a cold' (but 'recover from a cold').
vocabulary.note: Also used for problems and feelings: 'get over a break-up'.

listening.title: I think I'm coming down with something
listening.context: Daniel isn't feeling well. He goes into a pharmacy and asks the pharmacist, Helen, for advice.

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: Hi there. How can I help?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Hi. I think I'm coming down with something. I've had a sore throat since yesterday, and this morning I started coughing.

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: Oh dear. Have you got a temperature?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: I'm not sure. I feel quite hot, and I felt a bit dizzy on the bus this morning.

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: OK. Any other symptoms? A runny nose, or a headache?

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Just a bit of a headache. Nothing serious.

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: Well, to be honest, it sounds like a bad cold. You don't need a prescription for that. You can take these painkillers — two tablets every six hours, but no more than eight a day.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Are they OK for me? I'm allergic to aspirin.

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: Don't worry, there's no aspirin in these. They're just paracetamol. And you should drink a lot of water and get plenty of rest.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: The thing is, I've got an important meeting at work tomorrow. Should I go in?

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: Hmm, I don't think you should. You ought to stay at home for a day or two, so you don't give it to your colleagues.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: Fair enough. How long does it usually take to get over a cold?

lines.speaker: Helen
lines.text: About a week. But if you still have a temperature in three days, or you feel worse, you should see a doctor.

lines.speaker: Daniel
lines.text: OK, I will. Thanks very much for your help.

vocabulary.definition: the way you live, including your work, food, exercise and free time

vocabulary.definition: how heavy someone or something is

vocabulary.definition: to stay away from something, or to try not to do something

vocabulary.definition: something special and nice that you give yourself or someone else, often food

vocabulary.definition: in amounts that are not too big

vocabulary.definition: having enough water in your body

phrases.meaning: a way to give advice by imagining you are the other person
phrases.whenToUse: For personal, fairly strong advice to friends and colleagues. Use 'were', even with 'I'.

phrases.whenToUse: With friends and family, especially when someone is ill or stressed. Too informal for a formal email.
phrases.example: You've had a hard week — take it easy this weekend.

phrases.whenToUse: At the end of a conversation or message to someone who is ill or busy. Warm and friendly.
phrases.example: Get some rest, and look after yourself!

writing.sample:
Hi Tom,

I had the same problem when I started working in an office, so I know how you feel! First of all, you shouldn't skip lunch. If you do, you'll eat a lot of snacks in the afternoon. Why don't you take a homemade lunch to work? It's cheaper and more nutritious. You should also keep a bottle of water on your desk to stay hydrated. Have you tried walking to work, or working out after work? Even a few short walks a day can boost your energy. And you don't need to give up treats completely — chocolate is fine in moderation!

Good luck, and look after yourself!

reading.title: From the Steppe to the Supermarket
text: For centuries, the traditional Mongolian diet was simple. Herders ate a lot of meat, especially mutton, and they had plenty of dairy products, such as airag, yoghurt and aaruul (dried curds). They didn't eat many vegetables, because it was difficult to grow them on the cold, dry steppe. This diet gave people the energy they needed for long, hard days outside in winter.

Today, most Mongolians live in towns and cities, and the way they eat is changing fast. Supermarkets in Ulaanbaatar sell food from all over the world, and many young people now choose instant noodles, fast food and fizzy drinks. These meals are quick and cheap, but they often contain a lot of salt, sugar and fat.

Doctors are worried. City life is much less active than life on the steppe, but many people still eat the same large portions of meat as their grandparents did. As a result, health problems such as high blood pressure and heart disease are becoming more common, even among people in their thirties.

There is some good news, though. Fresh vegetables are cheaper and easier to find than twenty years ago, and more families are growing their own in greenhouses. Health experts say people don't need to give up traditional food. Instead, they should eat smaller portions of meat, add more vegetables to dishes like tsuivan and buuz, and choose water or tea without sugar instead of sugary drinks.

listening.title: Ask the nutritionist
listening.context: Nomin calls a radio programme about healthy eating to ask the nutritionist, Dr Evans, a question.

lines.speaker: Dr Evans
lines.text: Hello, you're on Healthy Living. What's your question?

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Hi. Well, it's about my son. He's seven, and he refuses to eat vegetables. He only wants pasta and sausages.

lines.speaker: Dr Evans
lines.text: Ah, that's very common, so don't worry too much. Does he eat any fruit?

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Yes, quite a lot, actually. He loves bananas and apples.

lines.speaker: Dr Evans
lines.text: Good, that helps. My first piece of advice is: don't force him. If a meal becomes a fight, children usually eat less, not more.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: OK. So what should I do instead?

lines.speaker: Dr Evans
lines.text: Try hiding a few vegetables in the food he likes. You can chop carrots or spinach very finely and put them in a pasta sauce. He probably won't notice.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: That's a good idea. Anything else?

lines.speaker: Dr Evans
lines.text: Yes. Let him help you cook. Children who help to make a meal are much more likely to try it. And you shouldn't give him snacks just before dinner, so he's hungry at the table.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Right. To be honest, he has a lot of snacks in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: Dr Evans
lines.text: Well, maybe cut down on those, and give him some raw vegetables instead — cucumber or carrot sticks with a dip.

lines.speaker: Nomin
lines.text: Brilliant. Thanks so much. I'll try that.

phrases: In my family, we eat a lot of…
writing.sample: In my family, we eat a lot of meat, like most Mongolian families. My mother cooks almost every day, so we don't eat much processed food, but our portions are quite big. We usually have rice or noodles with dinner, and we drink a lot of milk tea. We don't eat many vegetables in winter because they are expensive, but in summer we buy plenty of fresh cucumbers and tomatoes. My father loves sugary drinks, and I think he should cut down on them. I also think we ought to eat more fish and less salt. One easy change for me is breakfast — I often skip it, and I really shouldn't.

speaking.prompt: Some people say that eating healthily is too expensive and takes too much time. Do you agree? Give reasons and examples.
speaking.promptMn: Зарим хүмүүс эрүүл хооллох нь хэтэрхий үнэтэй, их цаг шаарддаг гэж ярьдаг. Та санал нийлэх үү? Шалтгаан, жишээ дурдаарай.
speaking.sample: I partly agree. In Ulaanbaatar, fresh fruit and vegetables can be quite expensive, especially in winter, and fast food is everywhere, so it's easy to eat badly. But I don't think healthy food always costs more. For example, soup with a few vegetables and a little meat is cheap and nutritious. The bigger problem, in my opinion, is time. People work long hours and don't want to cook in the evening. I think we should plan our meals for the week and cook a lot of food on Sunday. Then we can eat homemade food every day without spending much money or time.
